P1.evidence: Setter notes were referenced but only in the vaguest terms — 'Kim, that you spoke to, told me a little about you, so it seems that you're doing a lot' — which gave the prospect nothing to feel seen by, and he immediately had to explain his own situation from scratch. No four-part frame and no frame agreement. The open question ran cleanly: 'so, like, how can we actually help you with?'

P2.evidence: The best injury screening in the batch and the reason no clinical flag is raised here. The rep asked directly — 'Do you feel like you have any limitations, any injuries after years of playing sports?' — followed up on the answer, probed hips and stiffness specifically, and confirmed with 'But no serious injuries whatsoever?' getting an explicit 'No serious injuries. Nope.' Work was asked and pursued to sitting behaviour ('You sit a lot?'). Training week, results and nutrition were covered in real depth. Age was confirmed rather than asked, height and weight were volunteered. Sleep was raised only as an assumption about the baby and closed immediately. General and hereditary health conditions and daily energy were never asked.

P3.evidence: Strong. The rep refused the aesthetic answer twice — 'Why? What for?' and 'the main question I ask, like, why? Because is the juice worth the squeeze?' — then ran a genuinely good future-projection: 'So what does like 45-year-old Julian looks like?' The impact question landed hardest: raising the daughter growing up and not sitting on the sideline drew '100%. Yeah, that's a total, that's a great point' and unlocked the real material — wanting more children, wanting to race a future son on his birthday, and his own older parents who could not play basketball with him in the driveway. The reflect-back was present but thin: 'you're here to learn and to be like to play the long-term game.'

P4.evidence: Past attempts were covered thoroughly — Maximilian Moves via the Playbook app, traditional split training, the chiro and physio programme — and what happened with each was established. But the root-cause half of this phase does not apply cleanly: nothing failed for this prospect. His current solution works and he said so, 'I think I could do Max's program... and be fine forever.' That makes P4c and P4f unreachable rather than missed. The ceiling question was asked ('Do you feel like you've kicked like a ceiling with that weight right now?') but the gap was named by the rep rather than the prospect — 'nobody is watching your form' — which is the weaker version of P4e.

P5.evidence: The only consequence frame attempted was an injury-risk one, and it was the right instinct for this prospect: 'nobody is telling you, like, if your swing is, like, creating a compensation pattern, for example, for the hips or the lower back... it can result in an injury' and 'the subtle technical errors that feel fine until they don't.' It was never converted into a cost of inaction — no two-year question, no willing-to-settle, no why-not, no line in the sand. Genuinely hard here, because the prospect's status quo is working and he knows it, but that is exactly when the phase matters most and it was left at one observation.

P6.evidence: The belief question was never asked — whether he believes he can get there with the right structure and the right person in his corner. The all-in question was asked well: 'if we can figure out the details, like are you fully committed to showing up for this and doing the work to become the best 60-year-old that could be?' The answer was explicitly conditional — 'totally just depending on pricing... it's just a monetary thing. See if it makes sense' — which is precisely the hesitation the script says to return to Phase 5 on. Instead the rep went straight into the price menu, and the call never recovered.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and no payment was collected. The only money asked for was a $100 deposit to hold a follow-up call, which was refused. Steps 2 to 4 unreachable with no sale.

objection_plays.detail: The diagnostic move was excellent and better than the script asks for: 'is that you don't feel like there's value in that for 6K for you, or you don't have that amount?' That correctly separated value from capacity and got a clear answer — value. From there the play collapsed. Because this was not a capacity objection, the scripted financial picture would have been wrong to run and correctly was not, but nothing replaced it: no value build against the incumbent programme, no should-I-versus-how reframe, no isolate. The rep discounted instead, offering an unlisted three-month tier at $4,000, which conceded the value argument rather than winning it and is separately logged as a pricing deviation.

Opened by dismissing it outright — 'Come on, man, don't give me the wife objection' — which is the opposite of the play. One scripted move then ran, the obstacle check, and it produced a useful answer: she would not be opposed, she trains with him, it would benefit her too. That answer was never used. The rep did not ask whether, money aside, he personally believed it could get him there; did not test whether this genuinely needs her input or is permission to bet on himself; did not use the not-a-joint-decision frame. Note the scripted deposit-and-refund fallback did appear, but mutated: it was applied to booking a follow-up call rather than to the purchase, and framed as calendar scarcity rather than as a commitment device, which is what made it land as a charge for the rep's time.

Triggered clearly — 'something I want to think about, too. I'm not going to just commit to spending 4K with you here on the first call' and later 'let me go back and think about it and step away'. Two moves in the right spirit ran: 'Why not? You feel good about it' and 'Where's the missing piece you're not telling me?', the latter producing the real answer about opportunity cost of capital. None of the scripted language followed — no can-it-get-you-there, no thinking-versus-deciding, no the-way-you've-been-approaching-this, no identity move, no final are-you-sure. The play was abandoned in favour of the deposit ask.

Timing surfaced at the end — 'for right now, I'm okay for the time being' and 'shoot me a followup in a few months, something like that'. No move was run against it. The rep accepted a two-day callback window instead, having already spent his leverage on the deposit ask.

Script gap, and the central one on this call: a cheaper alternative that genuinely worked. The prospect has trained five days a week for over a year on Maximilian Moves' programmes through the Playbook app, has progressed to a 40lb bell on every movement, and stated plainly 'I think I could do Max's program for account macros and just keep going up in kettlebell weight and be fine forever.' Objection C assumes capacity to pay is the blocker; here the blocker is a functioning low-cost substitute delivering most of the outcome. This is the identical gap already logged against the Badrane Hriouch call and it now has a second, stronger instance. The playbook needs a value-differentiation play — form correction, programming knowledge transfer, movement library breadth — none of which was argued.

Script gap: virtual versus in-person delivery. The prospect said the decision would be entirely different if training were in person and that he would pay more for it — 'I would definitely be willing to spend more money on something that was like in person as opposed to something virtual.' The rep agreed rather than defending remote delivery — 'That would be totally different price range too' — conceding that the product is worth less than an in-person alternative at the moment of the price objection. There is no scripted defence of the remote model and there should be.

Script gap: the prospect self-diagnosing as outside the ICP. He raised it himself from the intake questions — that the offer seemed 'more so suited for people that are looking to make like a serious change as opposed to the minuscule things that I'm looking to do.' The rep asserted both segments are served and offered one anecdote. There is no scripted handling for an advanced prospect who believes the product is built for beginners, and this is a recurring commercial problem rather than a rep failure.

notes: Good discovery and the best injury screen in the batch, undone at the price. The prospect gave a conditional answer to the commitment question and the rep presented anyway instead of returning to Phase 5, then met a value objection with a discount — a new three-month tier at $4,000 — rather than a value argument. Coach two things specifically: treat 'depending on pricing' as hesitation, not as a yes; and build a real play for the prospect who already has a cheap solution that works, because discounting against Maximilian Moves at $4,000 still loses to him at app prices and simply reveals the list price as negotiable. The $100 deposit to book a callback should be stopped outright — it cost credibility with a prospect who was still engaged and turned a soft maybe into a decline.
